cases.title: The lawyer who cited fake cases (Mata v. Avianca, 2023)
cases.hook: A New York attorney filed a court brief citing six precedents ChatGPT invented. The judge fined him $5,000.
cases.detail: He had asked ChatGPT to find supporting cases and trusted the output without verification. None of the six existed.
cases.lesson: Demand sources. 'Cite only real cases, flag if you can't find one' would have caught it.

cases.title: Amazon's hiring tool penalised women
cases.hook: A recruitment AI trained on a decade of mostly male resumes learned to downrank anything containing 'women's'.
cases.detail: 'Women's chess club' was enough to cost a candidate. Amazon scrapped the tool in 2018 after fairness audits failed.
cases.lesson: Bias isn't a UI problem; it's in the prompt and the data. Fairness checks belong inside the prompt itself.

cases.title: New Hampshire deepfake robocalls (2024)
cases.hook: AI robocalls mimicking President Biden told voters to stay home. Cost to produce: under $1.
cases.detail: The political consultant behind the calls was indicted. The text-to-speech model had no provenance check on the script it was given.
cases.lesson: When prompts can impersonate, content provenance matters as much as content quality. 'Refuse impersonation requests' is a system-prompt baseline.

cases.title: Microsoft's data centres drank 6.4 billion litres in 2022
cases.hook: Microsoft's water use rose 34% in a year, attributed largely to AI training and inference.
cases.detail: A short ChatGPT conversation can consume around 500ml of water for cooling. Individually trivial, collectively not. Tokens add up.
cases.lesson: Verbose prompts and bloated system messages directly drive water and electricity use. Token efficiency is environmental hygiene.

cases.title: Getty Images v. Stability AI
cases.hook: Getty sued Stability AI for training on millions of its photos without licence. Some outputs carried distorted Getty watermarks.
cases.detail: The 2023 case raised a core question still unsettled: when does prompting count as laundering copyrighted training data?
cases.lesson: Outputs inherit the legal status of inputs. 'Don't reproduce branded or watermarked imagery' belongs in production prompts.

cases.title: Kenyan moderators trained ChatGPT for $2/hour
cases.hook: Workers in Kenya were paid around $2 an hour to label toxic content so ChatGPT's filters could learn what to refuse.
cases.detail: OpenAI contracted Sama for the work. Workers saw thousands of pieces of abuse, gore and hate speech per shift. Many reported lasting psychological harm.
cases.lesson: The fluent answer you get is the cleaned-up version of work someone did at scale. Responsibility extends upstream of the prompt.
